children: By Staff Writer
President Bola Ahmed Tinubu has welcomed the Coca-Cola System’s proposed $1 billion investment in Nigeria, assuring local and international investors that the country remains open for business.
Tinubu gave the assurance on Monday in Abuja at the 75th anniversary celebration of the Nigerian Bottling Company Limited (NBC), held at the Bola Ahmed Tinubu International Conference Centre.

The President, who was represented by the Secretary to the Government of the Federation, Senator George Akume, said the Federal Government was implementing reforms under the Renewed Hope Agenda to make Nigeria’s business environment more predictable, competitive and investment-friendly.

He said: “Our message to investors, both Nigerian and international, is clear: Nigeria is open for business, and we are working to make the business environment more predictable, more competitive and more supportive of investment.”

Special Adviser to the Secretary to SGF, Mr. Yomi Odunuga in a statement on Monday in Abuja said Tinubu identified reliable power and infrastructure, clear and consistent regulations, efficient ports and logistics, access to foreign exchange and a tax system that encourages productive enterprise as critical factors influencing investment decisions.

According to him, the reforms being implemented by his administration are aimed at building a more productive and competitive economy, reducing dependence on imports, expanding domestic manufacturing and creating more opportunities for Nigerians.

“We are making difficult changes because we want a more productive and competitive Nigerian economy. We do not want to remain overly dependent on imported goods while our own productive capacity remains underdeveloped.
“We want to produce more, manufacture more, add more value locally and create more opportunities for Nigerians,” he said.

The President welcomed the Coca-Cola System’s announcement in 2024 of a potential $1 billion investment in Nigeria over five years, describing the commitment, coming after $1.5 billion invested in the country over the preceding decade, as a vote of confidence in the Nigerian economy.

He said the Federal Government was interested not only in the volume of capital invested in Nigeria but also in the impact of such investments on employment, skills development, local sourcing, technology transfer and domestic productive capacity.
“For this administration, that is what investment must mean. We are interested not only in the amount of capital that comes into Nigeria, but in what that capital does here.

“Does it create jobs? Does it strengthen Nigerian businesses? Does it develop skills? Does it increase local sourcing? Does it bring new technology and knowledge? Does it help us produce more in Nigeria? Those are the outcomes that matter,” Tinubu stated.

He urged international businesses to see Nigeria not merely as a large market for their products, but as a country where they could establish production operations, develop local talent and supply chains, and compete in African and global markets.
Tinubu also commended the Nigerian Bottling Company for its continued investment in production capacity, including new production lines at Asejire in Oyo State and Challawa in Kano State.

He challenged businesses and policymakers to deepen local content by developing Nigerian companies into reliable suppliers to major manufacturers, training young Nigerians to operate and maintain modern industrial equipment and progressively replacing imports with competitively manufactured Nigerian products.
The President pledged that the Federal Government would continue to improve policies, infrastructure and the regulatory environment to encourage investment and domestic production.

He, however, stressed that government alone could not drive the required economic transformation, urging the private sector to complement government efforts through investment, innovation, risk-taking and job creation.

“Government has a role to play. We will continue to work on the policies, infrastructure and regulatory environment required to support investment and domestic production. But government cannot do this alone.

“The private sector must also play its part. Businesses invest. Businesses innovate. Businesses take risks. Businesses create jobs. Our responsibility in government is to create an environment in which those things can happen,” he said.
Tinubu further emphasised the importance of human capital development, saying investment ultimately derives its value from the opportunities it creates for people.

He commended NBC’s Supply Chain Academy, established in 1996, which has trained more than 1,400 young people, as well as the company’s women empowerment initiatives and community interventions in areas including water and hygiene.
The President said Nigeria’s youthful population could become a major economic advantage if young people were equipped with relevant education, technical skills and opportunities.

He said his administration wanted young Nigerians to have opportunities to become entrepreneurs, engineers, technicians, professionals, innovators and manufacturers, stressing that human capital development, enterprise and job creation remained key pillars of the Renewed Hope Agenda.

The President acknowledged the difficulties created by the ongoing economic reform process, noting that Nigerians and businesses had made sacrifices and had been forced to adjust to changing conditions.
He, however, maintained that longstanding structural challenges in the economy had to be addressed to build a stronger and more competitive Nigeria.
“I know that the reform process has not been easy. Nigerians have made sacrifices, and businesses have had to adjust to changing conditions. We are not blind to these realities.
“But we also know that some of the structural problems in our economy cannot simply be wished away. They have to be addressed,” he said.

Tinubu reaffirmed the Federal Government’s readiness to welcome investors prepared to make long-term commitments to Nigeria, particularly companies willing to manufacture locally, develop Nigerian talent, strengthen local supply chains and contribute to host communities.

“We welcome investors who are prepared to take the long view. We welcome companies willing to produce in Nigeria, develop Nigerian talent, strengthen local supply chains, and contribute to the communities in which they operate. That is the kind of partnership we want between government and business,” he said.

Earlier, Tinubu congratulated the Board, Management, employees, distributors, suppliers and partners of NBC on its 75th anniversary, describing the company’s journey from a business established in Lagos in 1951 to a nationwide enterprise as an example of the possibilities inherent in long-term investment in Nigeria.

He noted that the Coca-Cola System generated an estimated $1 billion in value-added economic activity in Nigeria in 2024, supported more than 160,000 livelihoods across its value chain and purchased approximately $601 million worth of goods and services from Nigerian suppliers.

According to him, the figures demonstrate the multiplier effect of productive investment, creating opportunities for suppliers, transporters, engineers, technicians, distributors, retailers, farmers, financial institutions and other businesses.

Tinubu charged NBC and the Coca-Cola System to sustain their investments in Nigeria, continue developing Nigerian talent, deepen local supply networks and explore new opportunities for creating value in the country.

He expressed confidence that Nigeria could build an economy that produces and exports more, creates greater domestic value, develops globally competitive industries and equips young Nigerians for emerging technologies and jobs.

He said economic transformation required consistent policies, investment, infrastructure and confidence in Nigeria’s capacity, assuring that the Federal Government would remain committed to the reforms necessary to achieve the objective.

title: ZAWYA: Nigeria: Tinubu welcomes Coca-Cola’s proposed $1bln investment
